title: When everything feels urgent: sort it, then act

narration: Say it's Monday.
Maya has four requests.
All four say urgent.
beats.visual_intent: The presenter opens beside the board; four request cards appear in a stack, each stamped urgent.

grounding.claim: Maya and her four requests are an invented running example

narration: She works down from the top.
By Friday, what mattered most is still waiting.
beats.visual_intent: Ticks run down the list in arrival order while a clock moves to Friday; the one important card is left unticked at the bottom.

grounding.claim: working in arrival order leaves the important task waiting (the example's outcome)

narration: Urgent says how soon,
not how much it matters.
Research suggests we lean toward the nearer deadline.
beats.visual_intent: The word urgent splits into two labels drawn apart: how soon, how much it matters; a balance tilts toward the deadline side.

grounding.claim: urgency is about how soon, importance about how much it matters
research suggests people lean toward the nearer deadline over a bigger payoff

beats.misconception: the most urgent request is the most important one

narration: So ask two other questions.
How much difference will it make?
How much work will it take?
beats.visual_intent: Two questions written large on the board: Impact? and Effort?

grounding.claim: sort each task by how much difference it makes and how much work it takes

narration: Impact runs up, effort across.
The client reply: big impact, ten minutes.
beats.visual_intent: The two questions become axes drawn on the board; the client reply card lands high on the left.

grounding.claim: the matrix crosses impact with effort
the client reply's sizing is part of the invented example

narration: The budget report: big impact, days of work.
Expenses: small and quick.
A deck redesign: small, but slow.
beats.visual_intent: The other three cards land one by one on the same board: high right, low left, low right.

grounding.claim: four positions from high or low impact and effort
the tasks' sizing is part of the invented example

narration: Four zones, four moves.
Quick wins: do them first,
so the client hears back today.
beats.visual_intent: The board divides into four zones; the top left is named quick wins and the client reply gets a tick.

grounding.claim: high impact, low effort tasks are quick wins, done first

narration: Major projects: block time for them.
Switching tasks tends to cost time and accuracy.
beats.visual_intent: Top right named major projects; the budget report becomes one solid block in a calendar strip instead of scattered fragments.

grounding.claim: major projects are planned and scheduled, not started in scraps
switching tasks tends to cost time and accuracy

narration: Fill-ins: batch them into one spare slot.
Thankless tasks: decline or park them, openly.
beats.visual_intent: Bottom left named fill-ins with a batch bracket; bottom right named thankless tasks, the deck card set aside with a later tag.

grounding.claim: fill-ins are batched or wait
thankless tasks are declined or parked, openly

narration: Saying no isn't refusing.
Tie it to your priority:
I'm on the budget report this week.
Then offer a date, or a smaller version.
on_screen: I'm on the budget report this week.
beats.visual_intent: A reply note is drafted beside the board with an arrow to the budget report; two options are written under it: a date and a smaller version.

grounding.claim: tie a no or later to your current priorities
offer a specific date or a smaller version instead of a maybe

narration: Your turn.
Her manager wants a new analysis by Friday.
Big impact, two days. Where does it go?
beats.visual_intent: The presenter turns to the viewer; a new card arrives beside the board, unplaced.

grounding.claim: the manager's request is part of the invented example

recall.answer: major projects: block the time and ask which task gives way
recall.tempting_wrong: do it right now because it is urgent and from the manager

beats.delivery: pose it, then leave the pause

narration: Major projects.
She blocks time and asks which task gives way.
beats.visual_intent: The new card lands top right; a second block appears in the calendar strip and a question arrow points at the other cards.

grounding.claim: high impact, high effort work is scheduled
ask a manager which existing task should give way

narration: New request? Place it, then sort again.
Tomorrow, start with one quick win.
beats.visual_intent: The opening list returns, now in the board's order with ticks; a last card drops onto the board and the list reorders itself.

grounding.claim: place new work on the same matrix and sort again rather than work in arrival order
do quick wins first
